title: How far should the pads be?
summary: The wait of urgent cargo grows by {{r:standoff_pct}} of distance between the landing pads and the base, but close pads spray the base with ejecta.
notes: E20 pooled law at the typical fleet load (results/table_E20.csv) and the E20 siting model (results/E20_fit.json). Wording for LEAD to edit.

standoff_pct.label: Urgent wait per km of pad distance
standoff_pct.note: pooled fit of ln(urgent mean delay), 100 (e^b - 1) per km of pad standoff, at the typical fleet load (experiment E20)

standoff_lo.label: Lower end of its interval
standoff_lo.note: lower end of the 95 % bootstrap interval over seeds

standoff_hi.label: Upper end of its interval
standoff_hi.note: upper end of the 95 % bootstrap interval over seeds

fit_years.label: Simulated years in the fit
fit_years.note: rows of the pooled fit: one seed of one cell each (E17 + E18)

keepout_pct.label: Urgent wait per km of keep-out radius
keepout_pct.note: per km of plume keep-out radius

miss_pct.label: Urgent wait per e-fold of landing miss
miss_pct.note: per e-fold of the mean landing miss

impacts_near.label: Ejecta impacts per landing, nearest pads
impacts_near.note: ejecta impacts on the base per landing at a 0.5 km standoff, Modelled from the Wittal et al. (2022) anchors

impacts_far.label: The same, farthest pads
impacts_far.note: the same at a 5 km standoff

far_cheapest.label: Cells where the farthest pads cost least
far_cheapest.note: share of the fleet and dispatch cells whose cheapest standoff is 5 km, at energy 500 $/kWh, damage 1 M$ per impact, delay valued at 100 $ per item-hour (prices Assumed)

steps.title: Every kilometre costs time
steps.text: Rovers carry each delivery from the pads to the base. The mean wait of urgent cargo grows by {{r:standoff_pct}} of standoff, with an interval of {{r:standoff_lo}} to {{r:standoff_hi}}.
steps.visual: The base and its two landing pads, with the rover routes between them drawn on the ground.

steps.title: Where the law comes from
steps.text: One fit over {{r:fit_years}} from {{r:fit_seeds}}: every fleet size, job rule, landing accuracy and pad size of the study.
steps.visual: The whole base from above, rovers driving between pads, depot and work sites.

steps.title: Keep-out zones barely matter
steps.text: Clearing a plume keep-out zone during each landing changes the wait by {{r:keepout_pct}} of keep-out radius, an interval of {{r:keepout_lo}} to {{r:keepout_hi}} that includes zero. The fleets are idle most of the time and absorb the evacuations.
steps.visual: A ring around the active pad marks the plume keep-out zone; rovers wait outside it until the lander is down.

steps.title: Landing accuracy acts through the pad edge
steps.text: Each e-fold of the mean landing miss adds {{r:miss_pct}}, because landings off the pad mean longer, rougher drives.
steps.visual: Touchdown points scattered around the pad; the ones outside its rim are highlighted.

steps.title: Close pads spray the base
steps.text: A landing blasts regolith outward. At the nearest standoff studied the model expects about {{r:impacts_near}} ejecta impacts on the base per landing; at the farthest, {{r:impacts_far}}.
steps.visual: The ejecta fan from a landing on the near pad reaching the base buildings.

steps.title: So: far, unless energy is dear
steps.text: Pricing hauling, ejecta damage and waiting time together, the farthest standoff studied is cheapest in {{r:far_cheapest}} of the cells at middle prices. Only cheap damage, together with dear energy or highly valued time, pulls the pads closer.
steps.visual: The base from a distance, with the pads at the far end of their routes.
